extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, lawmakers, USPTO officials, university tech-transfer offices, and industry stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Legislative-history guidance and interpretive standards for prior-user/prior-commercial-use defenses, post-grant/transitional review (Section 18), IPR/PGR coordination with litigation, joinder/consolidation rules, intervening rights, supplemental examination, and related PTO procedures under the America Invents Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting of prior-use rights / definition of internal commercial use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior use rights shall vest when innovative technology is first put into continuous internal use in the business of the enterprise with the objective of developing commercializable products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to cover internal uses that demonstrate a commitment to develop products; examples include agricultural breeding tools used seasonally or prototype-heavy R&D (Edison's multiple failures). The sponsor's intent is that reduction to practice plus diligent steps to maintain continuous, regular commercial use in manufacturing operations will create the defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for PCU defense (one-year rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as the prior use begins more than 1 year prior to the effective filing date of a subsequent patent or publication by a later inventor, the initiation of continuous internal use should guarantee the defense of prior use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must show commercial use at least one year before the patentee's filing or disclosure; this is the House compromise addressing university concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous internal use qualifies despite prototype failure
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuously used process qualifies as internal commercial use despite the fact that many prototypes will fail to have commercial merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R&D that produces many failed prototypes but is part of a continuous business activity to develop products still counts; testing and long-term field trials do not defeat continuous-use characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of PCU defense — limited license to prior commercial use
rubrics_metrics.description: The defense does not create a general license with respect to the patented invention, but rather only allows the defendant to keep making the infringing commercial use that he establishes that he made 1 year before the patentee’s filing or disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words 'subject matter' refer to the infringing acts, not the whole patented invention. Subsection (e)(3) permits increasing quantity/volume of the established use and allows improvements that do not further infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCU covers manufacturing processes and internal-use products
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCU defense is principally designed to protect the use of manufacturing processes and is expanded beyond processes to also cover products that are used in a manufacturing or other commercial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes closed-factory tools, substances exhausted in process, and internally-used customized software (e.g., HR systems) provided the use is integrated into an ongoing commercial process and not merely fleeting, experimental, or incidental. Consumer products sold to the public generally do not need PCU because public sale makes them prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal nature and third-party use — 'directed' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The final bill limits assertion of the defense for third-party uses to those third-party commercial uses that the defendant actually instructed the vendor or contractor to use, using the word 'directed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replaces broader 'caused' language to avoid covering vendor uses made without instructions or contemporaneous knowledge; 'directed' requires evidence defendant affirmatively instructed vendor/contractor in manner of work or use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entities covered by PCU — control/affiliate language
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (e)(1)(A)’s reference to entities that 'control, are controlled by, or under common control with' the defendant borrows established statutory usage of 'control'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black's Law Dictionary defines 'control' as direct or indirect power to govern management and policies (ownership, contract, or otherwise); analogous statutory definitions cited. Thus uses by controlled entities may be imputed where control exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: University and tech-transfer carve-out
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCU defense does not apply to patents owned by a university 'or a technology transfer organization whose primary purpose is to facilitate the commercialization of technologies developed by one or more such institutions of higher education.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to mirror Bayh-Dole 'primary functions' concept; extended to include university technology-transfer organizations (e.g., WARF). Exception to the exception exists where federal funding prohibitions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment / seasonal use clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (e)(4) barring assertion of the defense if use of the subject matter has been abandoned should not be construed to necessarily require continuous use of the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal or periodic use is acceptable; if a subject is so used (periodically/seasonally), its use has not been abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reduction-to-practice showing required for PCU
rubrics_metrics.description: The final bill drops the requirement of a showing of a reduction to practice that previously appeared in subsection (b)(1), because the use of a process or product in a commercial process will always constitute a reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative change removes a prior formal reduction-to-practice predicate; commercial use suffices as reduction to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional/post-grant review purpose and non-harassment intent (Section 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 is intended to enable the PTO to weed out improperly issued patents for abstract methods of doing business, and is not intended to allow owners of valid patents to be harassed or subjected to substantial cost and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history directs USPTO to implement Section 18 to avoid harassment; the program modeled on proposed post-grant review but with protections to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation standard for post-grant/transitional review — 'more likely than not' threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: To initiate a post issuance review under the new post grant or transitional proceedings, it is not enough that the request show a substantial new question of patentability but must establish that 'it is more likely than not that at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heightened requirement was created to make the procedures harder to use for harassment and is a higher standard than earlier reexamination thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitations on post-grant proceedings — no re-litigation of previously-considered issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that bars the PTO from reconsidering issues previously considered during examination or in an earlier reexamination still applies; while prior district court decisions do not strictly preclude PTO consideration, PTO must consider the court's decision and deviate only to the extent reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO expected not to initiate proceedings where petitions do not raise a substantial new question beyond earlier proceedings; avoid rehashing prior art/issues already considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive standards for evaluating claims in post-grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: In post-grant proceedings, claims should typically be evaluated to determine whether they meet the enablement and written description requirements of the act, and contain patentable subject matter under the standards defined in the statutes, case law, and as explained in relevant USPTO guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation follows existing statutory and case-law standards, and USPTO guidance; includes consideration of patentable subject matter doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological invention exception to Section 18
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 specifically exempts 'patents for technological inventions' from the new review at the USPTO — patents whose novelty turns on a technological innovation over the prior art and are concerned with a technical problem solved with a technical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciting technology alone does not exclude a patent; exclusions target inventions that merely use known technology to accomplish a novel business process. Examples: machinery to count/sort/authenticate currency excluded from review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of IPR/PGR with civil litigation (timing and stays)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill bars a party or his real party in interest from seeking or maintaining an inter partes or postgrant review after he has filed a declaratory-judgment action, but allows a declaratory-judgment action to be filed on the same day or after the petition for IPR or PGR was filed; such a declaratory-judgment action will be automatically stayed by the court unless the patent owner countersues for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to allow accused infringer to file first and be presumptively entitled to choice of venue while preventing forum-shopping or parallel resolution that undermines IPR/PGR processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline to seek IPR after being sued — one-year period
rubrics_metrics.description: The final bill extends the deadline for allowing an accused infringer to seek inter partes review after he has been sued for infringement from 6 months to 1 year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension recognizes difficulty in early litigation to identify relevant claims and accommodates defendants facing multiple vague claims; important given enhanced estoppel effects of IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening rights in IPR/PGR and claim amendment limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill extends intervening rights to inter partes and post-grant review; the bill does not allow new matter to be introduced to support claims in IPR and PGR and does not allow broadening of claims in those proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant to section 252: damages accrue only from the date of the conclusion of review if claim scope has been substantively altered (including narrowing). Intervening rights protect parties who acted on a challenger’s reasonable judgment that narrowing would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination — referral for 'material fraud' and materiality standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The new subsection provides that the Director shall refer to the U.S. Attorney General any 'material fraud' on the Office that is discovered during the course of a Supplemental Examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating whether a fraud is 'material' for purpose of referral, the Director should look to the Federal Circuit’s decision in Therasense: materiality required to establish inequitable conduct is but-for materiality (would the PTO have allowed the claim had it known the reference?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder and consolidation barred where only commonality is same-patent infringement (Section 299)
rubrics_metrics.description: New section 299 bars joinder of accused infringers as codefendants, or consolidation of their cases for trial, if the only common fact and transaction among the defendants is that they are alleged to have infringed the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to prevent circumvention of joinder limits by consolidation under Rule 42; adopts a common standard for joinder and consolidation to permit unrelated defendants to insist on separate trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period/public availability interpretation under new section 102
rubrics_metrics.description: To trigger the bar in new 102(a) an action must make the patented subject matter 'available to the public' before the effective filing date; public uses and sales are prior art only if they make the invention available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inventor's action triggers 102(a), it inherently triggers the grace period in 102(b). Congressional intent and committee reports support reading 'otherwise available to the public' as limiting prior art to things that make the invention publicly available; once in public domain it cannot be withdrawn.
